title: Early 21st Century Romanticism

jokes.text: Why does being a librarian make her even hotter? They're keepers of knowledge. She holds the answers to all of our questions, like, 'will you marry me,' and 'why are there still libraries.'
jokes.setup: Characters are ogling a librarian and riffing on why librarians are attractive — 'keepers of knowledge'
jokes.punchline: The 'questions' escalate from romantic ('will you marry me') to nihilistic ('why are there still libraries'), undercutting the romantic premise with absurdist irrelevance
jokes.explanation: The two-part list joke is well-structured: the first item ('will you marry me') is a predictable romantic beat, then the second ('why are there still libraries') is a sharp tonal left-turn into existential absurdism. It's efficient and characterful — this kind of deadpan non-sequitur is very Abed/Troy. The joke also does double duty as social commentary on library obsolescence without belaboring it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Will you marry me? You're the keeper of all knowledge, the guardian of wisdom itself.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's sweet, but... do libraries even exist anymore?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm serious. When was the last time you went to one?

jokes.text: I wanna be a book. She can pick me up. Flip through my pages. Make sure nobody drew wieners in me.
jokes.setup: Troy is fantasizing about the attractive librarian in increasingly literal terms
jokes.punchline: The fantasy escalates to wanting her to 'make sure nobody drew wieners in me' — a hyper-specific, childlike image that completely deflates the romantic setup
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. Troy's voice is pitch-perfect here — the escalating metaphor starts romantically ('pick me up,' 'flip through my pages') then crashes into something both childlike and oddly specific ('drew wieners in me'). The humor comes entirely from character: only Troy Barnes would express a romantic fantasy in terms of library book maintenance. The specificity of 'wieners' versus a more generic crude word is a deliberate craft choice that makes it funnier. Highly quotable, and the image is vivid and original.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You're like a book I want to read over and over again.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's sweet, but also kind of clingy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well, you're a really good book!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Now you're just describing a book.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: A book... with really nice illustrations.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Are you saying I have nice illustrations?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Really nice ones. But here's my concern—what if someone draws wieners in you?

jokes.text: Hey, maybe if we're too loud, she'll shush us. Okay. Books!
jokes.setup: Troy suggests they be loud enough to get shushed by the librarian as an excuse for interaction; Abed immediately tests the theory by yelling 'Books!'
jokes.punchline: Abed's instant, literal compliance — shouting 'Books!' — is the most socially awkward possible execution of the plan
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the joke is set up and paid off in four words. 'Books!' is exactly the kind of hyper-literal, socially oblivious thing Abed would shout. The humor is fully character-driven: Abed treats human courtship as a system to be executed mechanically. The follow-up 'Pretend like you're asleep' adds a beat of absurdist self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about ways to interact with the librarian. What if I get her to shush me? That could be flirtation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not flirtation, that's just you being annoying.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, think about it. The shush is intimate. It's personal. She's literally telling me to be quiet, which means she's aware of me.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Or it means she wants you to leave her alone.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Same thing.

jokes.text: Well, I don't believe in dibs or love at first sight or love or best friends or doing things.
jokes.setup: Troy asks Jeff for romantic advice about competing with a friend over a girl
jokes.punchline: Jeff's list of things he doesn't believe in keeps escalating — from 'dibs' to 'love' to 'best friends' to 'doing things' — a perfect encapsulation of his cynicism
jokes.explanation: The list joke is well-constructed with escalating specificity: 'dibs' (fair enough), 'love at first sight' (cynical but defensible), 'love' (darker), 'best friends' (troubling), 'doing things' (pure nihilism). The final item — 'doing things' — is the comedic peak, transforming Jeff from a cynic into something almost philosophically inert. It's very Jeff Winger and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Hey! HEY! We need help over here!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, we've been trying to get your attention for like five minutes!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: This is ridiculous, we're being as loud as—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Shh! Shh! The librarian's looking over here.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: *fake snoring*

jokes.text: You're gonna have to open your heart one day, Jeff. What happens if I don't? I miss the heart opening deadline? Valentine's Crapentine's.
jokes.setup: Troy sincerely warns Jeff about emotional unavailability; Jeff deflects with sarcasm about 'deadlines'
jokes.punchline: 'Valentine's Crapentine's' is Jeff's dismissive portmanteau for the holiday, delivered as a punctuation mark on his deflection
jokes.explanation: 'Heart opening deadline' is a solid piece of Jeff sarcasm — turning emotional growth into a bureaucratic task. 'Valentine's Crapentine's' is a decent wordplay gag but not exceptional; the joke that it's 'on his list' is a good button. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Jeff, I need relationship advice. What should I do?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well Troy, first you start by talking to her. Then you listen to what she says. Then you do things.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Things?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Romantic things. Thoughtful things. The things that make relationships work.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's actually pretty good advice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Of course it is. I'm very experienced at relationships. Mostly at ending them, but still.

jokes.text: Pierce, what was that? Gum. Why aren't you chewing? Because I'm using my mouth for this dumb conversation.
jokes.setup: Shirley spots Pierce has something in his mouth and suspects it's not gum
jokes.punchline: Pierce's reply — 'Because I'm using my mouth for this dumb conversation' — is simultaneously an admission and an insult, delivered with perfect oblivious confidence
jokes.explanation: Pierce's answer is funny on two levels: it's inadvertently self-incriminating (he's not chewing because a pill doesn't need chewing) and it's casually insulting to the person questioning him. The 'dumb conversation' kicker is a nice Pierce touch — his self-absorption turning a suspicious question into an inconvenience.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You really need to open your heart to people, Jeff. Let them in. Stop being so guarded all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, when's the deadline?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: There is no deadline, Jeff. It's not something you can schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you're saying I have until end of business?

jokes.text: Before you go barking up that tree, I have to tell you that she might not be interested... A friend of Ellen?
jokes.setup: Annie tries to tell Troy delicately that the librarian Page might be a lesbian
jokes.punchline: Troy's euphemism 'A friend of Ellen?' is an unexpectedly dated, almost sweet way of asking, contrasting with his usual directness
jokes.explanation: The 'friend of Ellen' euphemism is an affectionate period reference that plays on Troy's pop-culture-fluency. Annie then correctly names the word 'lesbian,' and the whole exchange is a gentle character moment with mild comedic payoff. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm really trying to open up here, and you're going to make a joke?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Sorry, sorry. You're right. Continue.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I just feel like... I need to let people in. Stop being so guarded.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's great. That's really mature.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I'm gonna add it to my emotional to-do list. Right after 'learn to cry' and 'stop being a narcissist.'

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You made a list?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I color-coded it.

jokes.text: Pierce, as someone who's been calling me a lesbian for the last year and a half, I'm sure that you don't have anything to say about me being friends with one. Nothing off the cuff. What I do have is a prepared statement.
jokes.setup: Britta preemptively calls out Pierce's expected homophobia, implying he'll stay silent
jokes.punchline: Pierce's response — 'Nothing off the cuff. What I do have is a prepared statement' — reveals he has thought deeply enough about his prejudices to draft formal remarks
jokes.explanation: This is a gem of character comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the 'nothing off the cuff' implies Pierce knows himself well enough to know his instincts are bad; (2) a 'prepared statement' suggests he has formalized his bigotry into bureaucratic form, which is both horrifying and hilarious; (3) it subverts the expectation that Pierce will say something immediately awful — he's actually prepared to be careful. This could only be Pierce. It sets up the payoff of the statement itself, and 'Nothing off the cuff' is a brilliantly specific phrase. Among the best written jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce, what are you chewing on?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Nothing! I'm not chewing on anything.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Your mouth is moving.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's just how my face looks now, okay? It's called getting old. You'll understand when you're not so annoyingly perfect.

jokes.text: 'And in summation, good luck... and bon appetit.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has been reading aloud a lengthy prepared statement about Britta's lesbian friendship; we now hear only the closing line
jokes.punchline: The statement ends with 'good luck and bon appetit' — an entirely inappropriate sign-off that suggests the preceding paragraphs were an incoherent tonal mess
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the 'prepared statement' joke is excellent. We've waited through a musical interlude (the song playing as a time skip) and the absurdity of the closing line — 'bon appetit' — does perfect work implying what we didn't hear. The formal document structure ('in summation') crashing into a food-service farewell is brilliantly incongruous. The fact that it's a callback makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Troy, Page might not be interested in you. She could be into women.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, into women? Like, she likes to hang out with them?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, Troy. Romantically interested in women.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh no. I thought you meant she had a thing for, like, female action movies or something.

jokes.text: Many, many paragraphs of that were oddly supportive. Wait till you hear the one I have for you.
jokes.setup: Britta reacts to Pierce's statement — which apparently had moments of genuine, if misguided, support
jokes.punchline: Pierce reveals he has prepared statements for each member of the group, turning what seemed like a one-off into a systematic behavioral modification program
jokes.explanation: A solid extension of the prepared-statement joke. 'Oddly supportive' is a great character note — Pierce's bigotry is so confused it accidentally becomes supportive. The reveal that he has one for each member elevates the joke from a one-off to a character revelation. Efficient and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So, uh, Britta... I heard you might be... you know... into girls?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, I'm... I'm... I'm... lesbian.

jokes.text: It was an awesome exit pill. Zip! Zop! Zooey! Bye!
jokes.setup: Shirley presses Pierce again about what was in his mouth; he finally admits it wasn't gum
jokes.punchline: Pierce calls it an 'awesome exit pill' and exits with a nonsensical verbal flurry ('Zip! Zop! Zooey! Bye!'), showing his pill-induced altered state
jokes.explanation: 'Awesome exit pill' is a great coinage — Pierce's matter-of-fact naming of recreational pharmaceuticals as functional accessories. 'Zip! Zop! Zooey!' is pure Chevy Chase / Pierce energy: a scat-like nonsense exit that doubles as a character state indicator. The callback to the gum bit pays off properly.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Pierce, I know what you're about to say, and I'm warning you—

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Actually, I prepared a statement. *pulls out paper* 'I, Pierce Hawthorne, do hereby acknowledge that my previous comments were inappropriate and hurtful. Going forward, I commit to being more thoughtful and considerate in my interactions with all members of this study group.'

jokes.text: He's recovering — dude can moonwalk! Now, I'm sure he's almost through his prescription. Besides, he's a baby boom. They invented drugs.
jokes.setup: The group discusses whether to intervene in Pierce's painkiller use; Jeff is dismissive
jokes.punchline: Jeff's excuse — 'he's a baby boom, they invented drugs' — is a hilariously glib historical generalization used to dodge responsibility
jokes.explanation: Jeff's reductive generational logic ('they invented drugs, so this is fine') is classic Jeff deflection — using a half-truth to avoid emotional engagement. 'He's almost through his prescription' as naive reassurance is also a solid line. Good character work, mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I have prepared a statement regarding Britta and the lesbian community. While some may find certain aspects of alternative lifestyles... unconventional, we must remember that tolerance and understanding are the cornerstones of a civilized society. Britta, we support you and your... choices. So bon appétit.

jokes.text: Yeah, they also invented TV. Have you seen him control one of those?
jokes.setup: Jeff argues baby boomers 'invented drugs' so Pierce is fine; Shirley counters with TV
jokes.punchline: The implication that Pierce can't operate a television undercuts the 'boomers are competent' logic — and is a genuinely specific, visual character detail
jokes.explanation: Very economical comeback. The logic is clean: Jeff uses one boomer achievement to excuse Pierce; Shirley counters with another boomer achievement Pierce can't handle. 'Have you seen him control one of those?' is a perfect kicker — it invites the audience to imagine Pierce baffled by a remote control, which is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I've prepared a statement. Britta, you are a woman of many talents and I respect you deeply.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wow, Pierce, that's... that's really sweet. Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I also have a prepared statement for Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Jeff, you are a terrible person and I hope you die.

jokes.text: He also listens to the Barenaked Ladies. Go get their dumb asses to help you.
jokes.setup: The group tells Jeff that Pierce listens to him; Jeff deflects
jokes.punchline: Jeff's suggestion that the Barenaked Ladies should do the intervention instead is absurdist deflection that also signals his contempt for the band — setting up the BNL argument
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the BNL running gag that escalates through the scene. The comedic premise — that the Barenaked Ladies are a credible authority figure who could conduct interventions — is absurd enough to be funny, and Jeff's contempt is well-calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce, what is that? Is that gum?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Gum? This isn't gum, it's a suppository. Whoop whoop whoop whoop!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Nyuk nyuk nyuk! Ooh ooh ooh!

jokes.text: Oh, okay. They're... they're BNL now. We use shorthand for the Barenaked Ladies. That's how fundamental they are. Yeah. Yeah!
jokes.setup: The group casually uses 'BNL' as shorthand; Jeff calls this out with mock incredulity
jokes.punchline: The whole group enthusiastically confirming that yes, BNL have shorthand status, as if this is self-evident, is the comedic peak of the exchange
jokes.explanation: The joke mines comedy from the gap between how the group treats BNL (with the reverence normally reserved for The Beatles) and what BNL actually is (a '90s Canadian alt-rock band). The group's synchronized 'Yeah. Yeah!' affirmation is a great moment of collective sincerity against Jeff's contempt. This is good Community — using a pop-culture reference as a prism for character dynamics.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yeah, but Pierce can't even use a computer. He thinks the internet is a series of tubes.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's not fair. Pierce is very tech-savvy for his generation.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Troy, last week he asked me how to 'turn on the Google.'

jokes.text: You know what Pierce probably needs more than anything? Some space. Maybe I do too... Maybe we all need some space to pull the knife out of the back of the most celebrated Canadian alt rock band of the mid-nineties, you selfish, jaded ass!
jokes.setup: Jeff uses 'Pierce needs space' as a pretext to remove himself from the intervention conversation; the group sees through it
jokes.punchline: Shirley's escalating defense of BNL climaxes with 'pull the knife out of the back of the most celebrated Canadian alt rock band of the mid-nineties, you selfish, jaded ass' — the absurdity of defending BNL with this level of emotional intensity
jokes.explanation: The BNL argument peaks here. Shirley's passionate defense — framing Jeff's dislike of a Canadian pop-rock band as a moral failing — is genuinely hilarious because of the disproportionate emotional investment. 'Pull the knife out of the back of the most celebrated Canadian alt rock band of the mid-nineties' is a brilliantly overwrought construction. The escalation from mild disagreement to 'you selfish, jaded ass' is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce listens to everything I say. I could tell him the Barenaked Ladies are the greatest band of all time and he'd believe me.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: They ARE the greatest band of all time!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: See?

jokes.text: This...is a fight! We...are fighting!
jokes.setup: The BNL argument has gotten surprisingly heated; everyone is emotionally engaged
jokes.punchline: Troy's announcement — delivered with apparent excitement and wonder — treats the group fight as a remarkable event rather than something to defuse
jokes.explanation: Perfect Troy moment. The deliberate pauses ('This...is a fight! We...are fighting!') turn a simple observation into something momentous, as if Troy is narrating a wildlife documentary about his own social life. It's pure character — Troy is both excited and slightly confused by the emotional intensity, treating the fight as a spectacle. Maximum economy, great character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Barenaked Ladies? Really? They're not even a real band.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Not a real band? Jeff, they've sold millions of albums! They're Canadian icons! Their wordplay is clever, their melodies are infectious, and 'One Week' is a masterpiece of rapid-fire pop perfection!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, they sing about how they like their eggs in the morning. That's not art, that's a breakfast order.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's whimsical! It's relatable! Not everything has to be dark and brooding to be valid!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: ...Did you just passionately defend a song about eggs?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yes. Yes, I did.

jokes.text: Now, you won't know this, being American, but tonight Liverpool are playing Manchester United. I am a stylish American, professor. I've been forcing myself to be into soccer since 2004.
jokes.setup: Professor Duncan tries to bond with Jeff over football (soccer), assuming Jeff won't know about it
jokes.punchline: Jeff's self-aware admission that he's been 'forcing himself' to be into soccer since 2004 — placing the effort in a specific, telling year (post-US World Cup hosting era) — is a perfect slice of aspirational American cultural posturing
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-description as 'a stylish American' who has been forcing soccer fandom is a sharp piece of observational character comedy. The specificity of '2004' sells the joke — it implies a calculated, image-conscious decision to adopt soccer fandom for social cachet. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The Barenaked Ladies are a legitimate Canadian rock band with multiple platinum albums!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, they're called the Barenaked Ladies. That's not a band name, that's a description of what happens at their concerts.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's completely unfair! And for your information, they have an acronym: BNL.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're telling me a band called the Barenaked Ladies needed to abbreviate their name? What were they afraid of? That people would figure out what 'barenaked' means?

jokes.text: You promised the study group? Whip, crack! I'll see you at precisely 6:30, or as the English call it, gravedigger's biscuits.
jokes.setup: Jeff mentions he has an obligation to the study group despite their fight; Duncan mocks him for it
jokes.punchline: 'Gravedigger's biscuits' as a fake English idiom for 6:30 — Duncan inventing nonsensical Britishisms with total confidence
jokes.explanation: 'Gravedigger's biscuits' is a brilliantly invented fake-British phrase. It's funny because it sounds just plausible enough that an American might wonder if it's real, while being clearly invented — 'gravedigger' and 'biscuits' have no logical relationship. Duncan delivering it with complete confidence is perfect. The 'whip, crack!' mockery of Jeff's group obligation also lands. Highly quotable and original.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I am NOT a control freak! I am a woman with standards, organizational skills, and a laminated color-coded filing system that would make the Library of Congress weep with envy!

jokes.text: Hey, thanks, buddy. Hey, Pierce! Hey, it's you! Yeah. The tiny man you see when you take enough pills.
jokes.setup: Pierce encounters a cheerful, small character (Magnitude) and greets him warmly
jokes.punchline: Magnitude's reply — 'The tiny man you see when you take enough pills' — reveals Pierce thinks he's a hallucination, which Magnitude takes completely in stride
jokes.explanation: This is a great multi-layered joke. It establishes Pierce's painkiller problem darkly (he has a 'tiny man' hallucination), introduces Magnitude as a character (we'll learn more later), and is delivered by Magnitude with zero judgment — which makes it funnier. The specificity 'when you take enough pills' is perfect. Dark but earned, fully character-integrated, and surprises on first watch.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We're having a fight!

jokes.text: Pierce, if doctors are so smart, why are there millions of 'em?
jokes.setup: Pierce tries to invoke his doctor's judgment to justify continuing his pills; Magnitude offers a counter-argument
jokes.punchline: 'If doctors are so smart, why are there millions of 'em?' — a perfectly constructed piece of fake logic that sounds like wisdom but is nonsense
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The joke works because it perfectly mimics the structure of folk wisdom ('if X is so smart, why Y') while the content is complete nonsense — there is no logical connection between being smart and being numerous. It's the kind of line that sounds profound for half a second before collapsing. The fact that it's delivered by a character who may or may not be a hallucination adds another layer. Maximum economy (12 words), highly original construction, massively quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: You don't know anything about soccer, do you?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know plenty about soccer. I watch it all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Name one player.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: ...Soccer players.

jokes.text: Look in your hand. [It's Valentine's, buddy. Be mine.]
jokes.setup: Magnitude (possibly a hallucination) directs Pierce to look at something in his hand
jokes.punchline: What's in his hand is presumably more pills or a drug-related object, with the 'Be mine' Valentine message making it a darkly comic addiction metaphor
jokes.explanation: Effective visual/dark-comedy moment. The Valentine's Day framing ('Be mine') applied to pills is a clever piece of dark irony — the drug as Pierce's Valentine. Mostly a visual/contextual joke that depends on what's in his hand, which we can only infer from the transcript.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I promised the study group I'd be here.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, it's half past the ferret now, so you're already seventeen minutes late in British time.

jokes.text: Are you the guys that keep staring at me and intermittently yelling out, 'books'?
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed approach Mariah the librarian with their formal romantic proposition
jokes.punchline: Mariah has noticed and remembered the 'Books!' outburst from earlier — their opening gambit has been witnessed and catalogued
jokes.explanation: Good callback. 'Intermittently yelling out books' is a nice comic formalization of what we saw — the word 'intermittently' is doing a lot of heavy lifting, implying this was not a one-time thing. The payoff confirms what was implied: they've been doing this repeatedly.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Let's meet at a quarter past the witching hour, shall we? That's roughly three-eighths of the way through a fortnight, in British time.

jokes.text: It is of utmost importance we protect that friendship from the stresses of courting you, so we're trying to be as direct and aboveboard about this as possible. Will you go to the dance with one of us, and if so, which one?
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy approach Mariah and lay out their romantic situation with Abed speaking for both
jokes.punchline: Abed's proposal is phrased as a formal business negotiation — 'utmost importance,' 'direct and aboveboard,' 'which one?' — turning romance into a contract discussion
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed comedy: treating a romantic approach with the clinical precision of a corporate proposal. The language ('utmost importance,' 'stresses of courting') is perfectly wrong for the context. This could only be Abed. The payoff — 'Will you go to the dance with one of us, and if so, which one?' — is a beautifully blunt multiple-choice question for romance.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wow Pierce, that moonwalk was incredible!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Thanks Chang. You know, I'm so high right now, I can't even tell if you're real or just a hallucination.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm real, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's exactly what a hallucination would say.

jokes.text: This is the cutest thing that's ever happened to me.
jokes.setup: Mariah receives Abed and Troy's formal, businesslike romantic proposition
jokes.punchline: Her reaction is not confusion or rejection but charmed delight — the audience's expectation of awkward failure is subverted
jokes.explanation: A solid subversion — we expect the formal approach to fail, but Mariah finds it adorable. The joke is in the gap between how weird the approach was and how warmly it's received. Functional misdirection, slightly underpowered as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know what? Doctors are just people. And some people are idiots. So statistically, some doctors are idiots. Your doctor might be an idiot.

jokes.text: Dude, I need to eat those tacos.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed step away to confer; they're carrying a briefcase
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a romantic negotiation, Troy's most pressing concern is eating tacos from a briefcase
jokes.explanation: The briefcase of tacos is a great background absurdist detail that gets its payoff here. Troy's urgency about the tacos mid-negotiation is true to character — he's easily distracted by food. Short, punchy, effective.

jokes.text: New proposal: Get to know us at the dance and decide there which of us you'd like to see again. Okay. Deal. Nice. What's in the briefcase? Oh. Tacos. You want one? No. Great. We really wanted them. Yeah. We're gonna eat them.
jokes.setup: The romantic negotiation is concluded; Mariah notices the briefcase
jokes.punchline: The deflation of the briefcase reveal ('tacos') and Troy/Abed's instant relief that she doesn't want any ('Great. We really wanted them.') is perfectly timed awkward comedy
jokes.explanation: The taco briefcase exchange is a small masterpiece of rhythm comedy. The rapid-fire Q&A ('What's in the briefcase? Tacos. You want one? No. Great. We really wanted them.') reads like a perfectly timed jazz improv. The humor comes from their immediate relief that they don't have to share and their eager announcement that they will now eat the tacos. Fully character-integrated and very rewatchable.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've conducted a comprehensive analysis of romantic compatibility metrics. Based on standard deviation curves and behavioral pattern recognition, I've determined optimal conditions for relationship initiation.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: However, I must note that human emotional variables remain largely unpredictable, which is frustrating because my spreadsheet only goes to column Z.

jokes.text: It's homophobic to ask questions? If you have to ask if it's homophobic to ask questions, haven't you already answered your own question? Have I? Don't know. Not a homophobe.
jokes.setup: Annie asks increasingly personal questions about Page; Britta calls her out for being potentially homophobic
jokes.punchline: Britta's circular logic ('if you have to ask if it's homophobic, you've answered your own question') is immediately deflated by her own admission 'Don't know. Not a homophobe.'
jokes.explanation: Good Britta moment — she deploys the kind of social-justice logic that sounds impressive but collapses under scrutiny, then immediately undercuts herself with 'Don't know. Not a homophobe.' The self-deflation is Britta's comedic signature: she reaches for moral authority and can't hold it. Well-structured exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What's in that briefcase?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We don't know.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're afraid to open it.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well, open it!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's just... office supplies.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Thank God. I thought we were gonna have to share it with everyone.

jokes.text: Should I ask her 500 questions about being a lesbian? Or should I just treat her like a normal person? That's a question you can ask.
jokes.setup: Annie, now self-conscious after Britta's lecture, asks how to act around Page
jokes.punchline: Britta's 'That's a question you can ask' validates the second option but the exchange reveals Annie's question was itself the right meta-question all along
jokes.explanation: Decent beat. Annie's earnest framing of the choice ('500 questions' vs. 'normal person') is slightly funny on its own, and Britta's approving sign-off is a good button. Mid-tier joke in the Annie/Britta dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So if you're a lesbian, does that mean you're only attracted to women, or...?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, it's more complicated than that. See, sexuality exists on a spectrum, right? So technically a lesbian could be attracted to someone who identifies as a woman but has masculine energy, or a woman who's exploring her gender identity, or even a non-binary person who presents femininely on certain days depending on the lunar cycle and their emotional availability.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So... yes or no?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Hi. I'm not a lesbian. Oh! I'm not either. Oh. But it's cool that you're friends with one.
jokes.setup: Annie and Page meet; both are operating under the assumption the other is a lesbian (or knows one)
jokes.punchline: Both simultaneously clarifying they're not lesbians, followed by Page's 'But it's cool that you're friends with one' — which is based on a false premise
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed farce beat. The mutual clarification ('I'm not a lesbian / I'm not either') in rapid succession is a classic comedy-of-errors moment, and Page's assumption that Annie has a lesbian friend (true, but for the wrong reasons) deepens the misunderstanding beautifully. Economical and structurally sound.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh! You're not the Dean's administrative assistant?

dialogue.speaker: Page
dialogue.line: Oh! You're not here about the parking violation?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh! So you ARE the Dean's assistant!

dialogue.speaker: Page
dialogue.line: Oh! Then YOU'RE here about the parking violation!

dialogue.speaker: Both
dialogue.line: Oh...

jokes.text: Page isn't a lesbian. She just likes hanging out with Britta, because it makes her feel cool to have a lesbian friend. But...Britta's not a lesbian. She thinks that Page is.
jokes.setup: The truth about the Page/Britta relationship is revealed
jokes.punchline: The double-reversal — Page thinks being friends with a lesbian is cool, but Britta isn't one; Britta thinks Page is a lesbian — is a perfectly constructed ironic knot
jokes.explanation: Excellent farce construction. The reveal is a double misunderstanding where both characters have the wrong information about each other, and the irony is rich: each is performing a social identity she doesn't have, for someone who is doing the same. This is tight plotting that also functions as sharp social satire about identity performance. The structure — a three-sentence explanation that lands perfectly — is well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you thought I was a lesbian?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, yeah. The way you dress, your short hair, how you're always talking about your feelings...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm just organized! And I have a thyroid condition!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so sorry. That's so offensive.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No, wait—I thought YOU were a lesbian.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? Why would you think that?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Because you're always going on about being progressive and alternative, and you wear those weird boots...

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: These are just boots, Annie!

jokes.text: Guess what, Annie. Page and I are going to the dance together. Hope I stay straight, right? Oh, sorry. My friend's a tad homophobic, so I was doing a bit.
jokes.setup: Britta announces she and Page are going to the dance; she thinks Page is a lesbian and is delighted to be making a progressive statement
jokes.punchline: Britta's 'I was doing a bit' aimed at Annie deflects onto Annie's supposed homophobia — but the real irony is that Britta is the one operating on a false premise
jokes.explanation: Good Britta irony — she's performing progressive allyship while completely misreading the situation. 'Hope I stay straight' as a 'bit' is Britta at peak Britta: trying to be edgy and cool while being totally wrong. The dramatic irony (we know the truth, she doesn't) adds an extra layer.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm just really embracing my lesbian identity right now.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Annie's the one who's actually confused about her sexuality, but sure, let's focus on me.

jokes.text: Yeah, 0-0. Electrifying.
jokes.setup: Duncan asks Jeff if he's worried about his phone; Jeff claims not to be and they watch the soccer match
jokes.punchline: Jeff's deadpan 'Electrifying' for a 0-0 soccer match is a perfect one-word American observation about the sport
jokes.explanation: One-word joke with perfect economy. The American complaint about soccer scores is familiar territory, but Jeff's flat 'Electrifying' has just enough character-specific sarcasm to elevate it. Not original, but very efficiently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: This is going to be the greatest soccer match of all time!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, it's currently 0-0, so I'm really on the edge of my seat watching two teams accomplish nothing.

jokes.text: Aw. Worried that your six-headed ball and chain will be calling? Fine.
jokes.setup: Duncan notices Jeff is resisting the urge to check his phone for messages from the study group
jokes.punchline: 'Six-headed ball and chain' as a description of the study group — combining the standard 'ball and chain' relationship metaphor with the specificity of six people
jokes.explanation: Nice coinage. 'Six-headed ball and chain' extends a familiar metaphor in a creative direction and accurately captures Jeff's relationship with the group from his perspective. Duncan's teasing is in character for him.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Calling his phone a slut

jokes.text: That's better, you big slut.
jokes.setup: Jeff turns off his phone (or puts it away) at Duncan's prodding
jokes.punchline: Duncan's affectionate 'you big slut' is a comically inappropriate term of endearment, delivered with warm British informality
jokes.explanation: Duncan's casual vulgarity in an affectionate context is a good character note — he has a very British-pub-friend energy that makes 'you big slut' land as warmth rather than insult. Short, punchy, funny in context.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Ha! Chang, like 'change,' because I'm always changing things up! Whoop whoop whoop whoop!

jokes.text: It's Chang! Chang? Why? I don't know! I can hear you guys.
jokes.setup: Chang unexpectedly appears at Jeff's door
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Duncan's panicked whispered exchange ('Chang? Why? I don't know!') heard by Chang standing right there ('I can hear you guys') is a classic comedy-of-manners beat
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom beat — characters talking about someone who can clearly hear them. The 'Why? I don't know!' panic is funny in its helplessness. Familiar structure but efficiently executed with good character energy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What's with all the British terminology?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, in Britain we have a word for everything. A lift is an elevator, a flat is an apartment, and a bathroom is a place where you go to take a bath, which is insane.

jokes.text: Ha! There it is! Man U. versus Liverpool! For God's sake, just let him in. He's wearing the right colors and everything.
jokes.setup: Jeff is resistant to letting Chang in; Duncan advocates for him
jokes.punchline: Duncan's reason for letting Chang in — 'he's wearing the right colors' — treats soccer loyalty as a sufficient character reference, overriding all concerns about Chang's creepiness
jokes.explanation: Duncan's tribal soccer logic overriding all practical concern is a good character moment. The 'right colors' as a character reference is a fun absurdist metric. Mid-tier joke with nice character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I want to order a pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, you'll need to use the pizza box.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: The pizza box?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Yes, everything means vagina.

jokes.text: Don't mind if I Chang!
jokes.setup: Jeff grudgingly invites Chang in
jokes.punchline: Chang's 'Don't mind if I Chang!' — a pun on 'don't mind if I do' using his own name — is delivered with maniacal self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: Name-pun jokes are a low bar, but 'Don't mind if I Chang' works better than average because it's characteristically self-aggrandizing — Chang inserting himself literally and figuratively. The pun works phonetically and the energy of delivery elevates it. Not high craft but charming.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang, just use the landline.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Alexander Graham Bell? More like Alexander Graham *Hell* — because that's where this conversation is going!

jokes.text: There's space for three fannies on this sofa. Hey. In England, fanny means vagina, right? In England, everything means vagina.
jokes.setup: Duncan invites Chang to sit on the sofa using the British word 'fanny' (meaning backside in British usage)
jokes.punchline: Chang correctly identifies the double meaning; Duncan's response — 'In England, everything means vagina' — is a sweeping absurdist generalization that escalates the joke
jokes.explanation: The 'fanny' double-meaning is a well-worn comedic mine, but 'In England, everything means vagina' is a great escalation that saves it from being too predictable. Duncan's confident, sweeping British cultural authority is funny, and the line is quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm a complete package. I've got everything you need.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: HBO, Showtime, premium channels, sports packages...

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm basically cable TV.

jokes.text: In England we call them Italian fannies. Landline? Okay, grandma Bell.
jokes.setup: Duncan extends the fanny joke to pizza; Chang makes fun of Jeff for having a landline
jokes.punchline: 'Italian fannies' extends the running gag with internal logic; 'grandma Bell' is a dated-tech insult that also makes a punny reference to Alexander Graham Bell
jokes.explanation: 'Italian fannies' is a decent extension of the running gag. 'Grandma Bell' is a mild joke — it works as a generational tech insult and the Bell reference adds a layer, but it's not especially sharp. Both are mid-tier jokes riding the energy of better material around them.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what? Let's give them something to really talk about.

dialogue.speaker: Page
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I mean, let's commit to a fake lesbian performance. Right here, right now.

dialogue.speaker: Page
dialogue.line: Wait, are you serious?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Completely serious. Let's do it.

jokes.text: Cellie... / Ah. Go use the landline. / Landline? Okay, grandma Bell.
jokes.setup: Chang goes to use his cell phone; Jeff tells him to use the landline
jokes.punchline: Chang's 'Okay, grandma Bell' — calling Jeff grandma-ish for having a landline — is a quick generational tech joke
jokes.explanation: Functional tech-generational joke. 'Grandma Bell' as a name for someone with a landline works fine, though the joke is fairly common territory. Sets up Chang's phone call which is funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Come on! That was a clear foul! What are you, blind?! That's complete bollocks! Absolute rubbish! You're a wanker, ref!

jokes.text: Star-burns, it's Chang. Remember that pizza you owe me? Well, it's time to pay up. Party at Winger's. Tonight.
jokes.setup: Chang uses Jeff's landline to call someone named Star-burns to organize a party at Jeff's apartment without Jeff's knowledge
jokes.punchline: Chang is calling in a pizza debt to stage a party at someone else's home — the audacity and elaborate nature of his plan is the joke
jokes.explanation: Chang calling in a pizza favor to throw a party at Jeff's apartment is a good escalation of his boundary-less behavior. The 'it's time to pay up' delivery makes it sound like an organized crime arrangement, which elevates the absurdity. The reference to 'Star-burns' as a known character with a pizza debt is fun world-building.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Well, hello there. I didn't know this was a party. Where's the music? Where are the girls?

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: You know, this reminds me of that scene in Blazing Saddles where—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, we're not doing this.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Leonard, no. Just... no.

jokes.text: So Mariah, what you get with me is the complete package... HBO, Showtime, Starz, Starz black.
jokes.setup: Troy is pitching himself to Mariah at the dance as the better choice over Abed
jokes.punchline: Troy pitches himself using cable channel tiers — framing himself as a premium subscription — and the specific inclusion of 'Starz black' is the peak absurdist detail
jokes.explanation: Troy's self-pitch as a premium cable package is a great metaphor — it's how he thinks about himself (maximum entertainment value) and it's characteristically Troy to use pop-culture shorthand for self-expression. 'Starz black' as the final, most specific tier is the comedic peak — it implies depth and variety but it's also just a minor premium channel, which deflates the metaphor slightly in a funny way.

dialogue.speaker: Magnitude
dialogue.line: Pop! Pop!

jokes.text: With all due respect to my friend here, if you go with me, you can expect this on the dance floor. [Troy's dance performance]
jokes.setup: Troy promises Mariah something exceptional if she chooses him, then demonstrates
jokes.punchline: Troy begins dancing — presumably impressively — as his closing argument in the romantic competition
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that depends entirely on the performance — Troy's dance is his trump card and presumably impressive given earlier moonwalk references. The transcript gives us the setup but not the full visual payoff. Character-consistent joke (Troy as dancer) with solid structural setup.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And that's why the Saw franchise represents a postmodern deconstruction of the American dream filtered through the lens of torture porn—which I've now spent the last six hours analyzing in excruciating detail.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've watched all seven films back-to-back and created a comprehensive breakdown of every trap mechanism and its symbolic relationship to Jigsaw's childhood trauma.

jokes.text: I feel like everyone's staring. Not that I care. Well, of course they're staring. They've probably never seen a straight girl and a lesbian so comfortable together. Exactly.
jokes.setup: Britta and Page are at the dance; Annie observes people staring at them
jokes.punchline: Britta's confident explanation for the stares ('never seen a straight girl and a lesbian so comfortable together') is based on her completely wrong understanding of the situation — Page is straight, Britta isn't a lesbian
jokes.explanation: Good sustained irony — the audience knows the truth (neither is a lesbian), making Britta's confident explanation richer. Annie's 'Exactly' endorsement when she actually knows the truth adds a layer of her going along with the farce. Well-integrated into the running misidentification plot.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Cool. Cool cool cool.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Here, Troy.

jokes.text: Those two were talking about us. Well, let's give them something to really talk about. Let's do it.
jokes.setup: Britta notices people watching them and suggests escalating
jokes.punchline: The implication is that they're about to do something provocative — presumably kiss or dance intimately — while both have fundamentally misread each other's sexuality
jokes.explanation: Good tension builder. The dramatic irony is at its peak here — both women are about to do something they think means different things. The brief, clipped dialogue ('Let's do it') is appropriately loaded. Works as a setup for the later reveal more than a joke in isolation.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Annie, you're a— you're a terrible person and I hope you die in a fire!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I took some of those pills that Jeff gave me. They're making me say terrible things.

jokes.text: Oh, nice call, ref! Bite my banger!
jokes.setup: Duncan watches soccer and gets frustrated with a referee call
jokes.punchline: 'Bite my banger!' as a British sports insult — 'banger' (sausage) used as an expletive substitute is a charmingly mild yet characteristically Duncan outburst
jokes.explanation: 'Bite my banger' is a funny coinage that plays on Duncan's British affectations and the 'everything means vagina' joke from earlier, while also being a food-based insult that's inherently mild. The character specificity is good — Duncan's soccer passion mixed with his British vernacular.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, we're really committed to this bit—

dialogue.speaker: Crowd Member
dialogue.line: You're disgusting! Both of you!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, that's... that's actually hurtful.

dialogue.speaker: Page
dialogue.line: Yeah, we were just joking around.

dialogue.speaker: Crowd Member
dialogue.line: Freaks! Go back to wherever you came from!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget it. This isn't funny anymore.

jokes.text: Jeff, something's up with your toothbrush, man. What the hell? I had to get cleaned up. Why?
jokes.setup: While watching soccer, Jeff is informed his toothbrush has been used
jokes.punchline: Chang has apparently used Jeff's toothbrush — again treating Jeff's personal space as his own — escalating his intrusion from driver's license to toothbrush
jokes.explanation: Chang's escalating boundary violations are a running theme in the episode and this continues that. The toothbrush is a specifically intimate invasion that ratchets up the cringe. Functional but not especially inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I didn't choose Abed because he's obsessed with that Saw movie franchise.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Abed's appreciation for the Saw films is actually a sophisticated study of how the series deconstructs American capitalism and examines the value of human life in a post-industrial economy. The traps aren't just torture devices—they're philosophical metaphors.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah! Pizza time! Leonard? Where are the white women at? No. There are no white women here, Leonard. This is not a party!
jokes.setup: Chang's unauthorized party starts materializing: pizza arrives, then Leonard shows up
jokes.punchline: Leonard's first words upon arrival — 'Where are the white women at?' — is a surreally inappropriate greeting that Jeff has to explicitly shut down
jokes.explanation: Leonard is used sparingly in Community but always to great effect. His arrival line ('Where are the white women at?') is hilariously inappropriate — both too forward and weirdly specific, delivered by an elderly man at an unsanctioned party. Jeff's escalating denial ('No... This is not a party!') is the straight-man punctuation.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: My date went terrible. She said my pop culture references were immature.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? That's insane! Pop culture IS culture!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Right? I mean, what's the difference between analyzing a Tarantino film and analyzing Shakespeare?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Exactly! And Shakespeare wrote about the same stuff anyway — murder, betrayal, people yelling—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: See?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, is Shakespeare pop culture? Is he? Because if he's not, I've been defending something I don't understand for three minutes.

jokes.text: Don't tell that to Magnitude. Who's Magnitude? Yo, yo, yo, yo, yo! Pop, pop! Bam!
jokes.setup: Jeff insists it's not a party; Chang references Magnitude as a partygoer
jokes.punchline: Magnitude's entrance — 'Yo yo yo yo yo! Pop, pop! Bam!' — is his entire personality distilled into an arrival, answering 'Who's Magnitude?' definitively
jokes.explanation: Magnitude's introduction is one of the episode's best moments. 'Pop, pop!' becomes a running gag and his entire character is established in three words. The joke is brilliantly economical: Jeff asks 'Who's Magnitude?' and the answer is not an explanation but a demonstration. Magnitude IS 'pop, pop' — his identity is his catchphrase, which is itself the joke about a certain type of party-energy character. Highly quotable and a genuine Community moment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Who is this guy?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: That's Magnitude. He's always saying 'Pop pop!'

dialogue.speaker: Magnitude
dialogue.line: Pop pop!

jokes.text: That's my analysis of the Saw movie franchise.
jokes.setup: Magnitude has just entered with 'Pop, pop! Bam!' energy
jokes.punchline: He announces that his energetic entrance was actually his critical take on the Saw horror franchise — a completely unexpected context for 'pop pop bam'
jokes.explanation: This is the best Magnitude joke in the episode. The punchline recontextualizes his entire entrance — 'Pop, pop! Bam!' was not exuberant greeting but film criticism, reducing the entire Saw franchise to onomatopoeia. It's a brilliantly absurdist meta-joke about both reductive film criticism and Magnitude's character (his catchphrase is so universal it applies to everything). The economy is stunning: one sentence rewrites everything before it. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: That about does it, so I think it's time for you to choose. [Troy and Abed present their case to Mariah at the dance]
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed have been courting Mariah at the dance with their characteristic methodical approach
jokes.punchline: Abed calling time on the courtship process with 'That about does it' as if completing a formal evaluation
jokes.explanation: Abed treating the romantic courtship as a formal process with a defined endpoint is consistent character comedy. The businesslike 'That about does it' as a close to a romantic pitch is a good detail. Mid-tier.

jokes.text: Cool. You can have this then. Thank you, Mariah. Have a great night.
jokes.setup: Troy tells Abed that Mariah chose him; Abed's reaction is awaited
jokes.punchline: Abed's response — giving the punch to Troy, politely thanking Mariah, and wishing her a great night — is a perfectly calibrated non-reaction that is funnier than any emotional outburst would be
jokes.explanation: One of the best Abed moments in the episode. The humor is in what Abed doesn't do — he doesn't react emotionally, doesn't sulk, doesn't make it awkward. He simply transfers the punch and exits gracefully. The understated 'Cool' followed by a polite farewell is completely Abed and deeply funny precisely because it's the socially appropriate response that most humans couldn't manage. The rewatch is rich because we're watching a character who may genuinely feel nothing, or who processes everything differently.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang, what are you doing in my apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh hey Jeff, I was just borrowing some stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Borrowing? Chang, you don't even live here!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yeah, but your underwear is really comfortable.

jokes.text: Pierce? You go straight to hell! Wh... Ha... Oh, I'm sorry, Annie. I've been... I don't know. I've been going through all these mood swings lately.
jokes.setup: Annie approaches Pierce at the dance, possibly to check on him
jokes.punchline: Pierce's unprovoked 'You go straight to hell!' at Annie — immediately followed by confused apology and blaming 'mood swings' — is a dark-comic encapsulation of painkiller-induced instability
jokes.explanation: Pierce's random aggression followed by genuine confusion about his own behavior is a solid dark-comedy beat. The painkiller subplot plays seriously but Pierce's volatility gives the show license for the unexpected attack on Annie. 'You go straight to hell!' at a sweet, concerned person is a good shock gag.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I've been living here for three months.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you've been living in the study room?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Where else was I supposed to go? My apartment got repossessed.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Chang, that's horrible.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's not so bad. I keep my clothes in the refrigerator and my shoes in the microwave.

jokes.text: Ha ha! Look at the lesbians. Lesbians! Screw you! Screw you!
jokes.setup: Britta and Page are at the dance; strangers make fun of them for being perceived as lesbians
jokes.punchline: Both Britta and Page fire back 'Screw you!' simultaneously — unified in their defiance, though the audience knows neither is actually a lesbian
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is at full strength here — both women defending an identity neither possesses. Their unified defiance is both funny (they're defending a false premise) and oddly endearing. The joke is more structural than line-based.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I got a pet. Two pets actually.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang, no.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I named one Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: So when I call 'Jeff!' one of them comes running. It's like having you, but obedient.

jokes.text: I don't care what they say. Oh, I don't either. I just wish it wasn't such an issue for them. Yeah, but that starts with us. It starts...With us.
jokes.setup: Britta and Page bond over standing up to homophobia
jokes.punchline: Their earnest 'it starts with us' moment — building to what appears to be a kiss — is predicated entirely on a misunderstanding; neither is what the other thinks
jokes.explanation: The 'it starts with us' escalation toward a kiss is a nice dramatic-irony peak — the most earnest possible framing for a moment that is completely built on false premises. The comedy is structural rather than line-based, but it works.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay everyone out! Out! I need this room cleared immediately. And I'm taking names. Leonard? Out. Vance? Gone. And you, what's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Background Character
dialogue.line: Uh, Quendra.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Quendra? Out! You too, Stacey Kimball Epstein. And Stacey Kimball Epstein's friend, Varnabicus.

jokes.text: I've never done this before. Me neither. Wait! What?
jokes.setup: Britta and Page are about to kiss; both express that they've never done this before
jokes.punchline: Page's 'Wait! What?' upon hearing Britta say she's never done this — implies Britta is straight, which breaks Page's understanding of the entire situation
jokes.explanation: Perfect farce payoff. The 'I've never done this' exchange is a classic comedy-of-errors unraveling — both women realize simultaneously that the other is not what they thought. The 'Wait! What?' is the comedic beat that cracks open the entire misunderstanding. Great economy and structure — the whole farce unravels in nine words.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I guess I'm like the Statue of Liberty. You know, I stand there looking all impressive, and troubled people just show up.

jokes.text: What was wrong with Abed? Well, I mean, he did talk about the Saw movies for two hours. Yeah, but there are eight of them, and they're two hours apiece, and the first one did redefine the genre, and... Troy, I would love to be his friend.
jokes.setup: Mariah explains why she didn't choose Abed — he talked about Saw movies for two hours
jokes.punchline: Troy begins defending the Saw franchise with increasing specificity ('eight of them, two hours apiece, first one did redefine the genre') — clearly agreeing with Abed's assessment — before Mariah cuts him off: 'I would love to be his friend.'
jokes.explanation: Very good joke that works on multiple levels: (1) Troy unintentionally reveals he would have had the same conversation; (2) Mariah's diplomatic 'I would love to be his friend' is a perfectly calibrated soft rejection that acknowledges Abed's value without pretending he's romantically viable; (3) it's a good character moment for Troy as the more socially adapted version of the Troy/Abed pair. The escalating Saw defense is characteristically Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No messages at all.

jokes.text: [Abed, alone, visibly processes the rejection] You know. [cut to:] I hate her, I hate her, I hate her, I hate her!
jokes.setup: Troy implies Abed has social limitations ('But romantically, he's...'); the sentence trails off; we cut to Abed
jokes.punchline: Abed's reaction — 'I hate her, I hate her, I hate her, I hate her!' — reveals he actually did have feelings, expressed in his own hyper-compressed, repetitive way
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. The 'You know' — the trail off about Abed's romanticism — is an already good joke (everyone agrees but nobody says it). But the cut TO Abed expressing 'I hate her, I hate her, I hate her!' is a beautiful subversion: Abed DID have feelings, he just processes them differently and reveals them in his own time. The repetitive hyper-expression ('I hate her' x4) is funny AND poignant. Perfect character integration — this is emotionally honest Abed comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what's scary? Change. You know what's a nightmare? Admitting you need help. But you know what's really terrifying? Admitting you need help and then actually following through with it. At least for me.

jokes.text: She called you weird! I am weird. Not as weird as her! Who the hell is Nicholas Nickleby? She wouldn't shut up about it.
jokes.setup: Troy defends Abed's rejection by attacking Mariah; Abed takes the news philosophically
jokes.punchline: The reason Mariah is apparently weird — she talked extensively about Nicholas Nickleby — is a mirrored version of the Saw critique (Abed talked too much about Saw, Mariah about Dickens) and also a funny specific choice
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure is elegant: Mariah rejected Abed for talking too much about Saw; Troy rejects Mariah for talking too much about Nicholas Nickleby. 'Who the hell is Nicholas Nickleby?' is a funny line in Troy's voice — he's defending his friend by showing Mariah is equally odd. The Dickens choice is nicely specific and implies Mariah is a 19th-century literature nerd, which mirrors Abed's horror-film expertise.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm gonna get in on this. I'm sensing an opportunity here.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Two young guys reconnecting? That's a growth market. I'm thinking a line of friendship bracelets, maybe some matching outfits.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: We could franchise it. 'Troy and Abed's Excellent Adventure Merchandise.' I'll handle distribution.

jokes.text: There's someone out there for us. Happy Valentine's Day. It is now.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy reflect on their romantic setback
jokes.punchline: The exchange is funny in its compressed, sitcom-perfect resolution — Troy's earnest 'Happy Valentine's Day' and Abed's 'It is now' as validation of their friendship
jokes.explanation: Sweet rather than hilarious — a landing-gear joke that closes the Troy/Abed romantic subplot with warmth. 'It is now' is a nice Abed line, minimalist and genuine. More affecting than funny, but it functions as a comedic beat with good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I have a confession to make. I've been unfaithful.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I cheated on my wife. It says right here on this card: 'Roses are red, violets are blue, I cheat because I love you.'

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's not what it says.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Then what does it say?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It says 'I cheat...to be with you.' It's about playing cards.

jokes.text: It's weird, but I've never heard of Magnitude before tonight. He's a one-man party! You're always busy with your study group. Well, he's not with them tonight.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Duncan acknowledge that Magnitude has taken over the apartment party
jokes.punchline: 'He's a one-man party!' — Duncan's description of Magnitude — perfectly encapsulates the character's comedic premise in four words
jokes.explanation: 'One-man party' is a great character summary and a kind of meta-confirmation that Magnitude's presence is itself comedic. The irony of Jeff missing Magnitude because he was 'always busy with his study group' adds a character note.

jokes.text: Pop, pop! Ha ho! Pop, pop! Pop pop pop pop pop pop! Pop pop pop pop pop pop!
jokes.setup: Magnitude continues his 'Pop, pop!' at the party; Duncan joins in
jokes.punchline: Duncan adopting 'Pop, pop!' — a British professor joining a one-man party's catchphrase in an escalating, drunken chant — is the running gag's comedic peak
jokes.explanation: The running gag payoff: a professor has been won over by Magnitude to the point of joining the chant. Duncan's corruption by 'Pop, pop!' is a funny character note, and the escalating mutual chanting is a good physical/vocal comedy moment.

jokes.text: I never said I was a lesbian. Why didn't you just ask me? Oh, what am I, a homophobe? I don't care about people's preferences. You so care.
jokes.setup: The farce unravels: Page reveals she never said she was a lesbian
jokes.punchline: Britta's defense — 'Oh, what am I, a homophobe? I don't care about people's preferences' — is immediately undercut by Page: 'You so care.'
jokes.explanation: The farce payoff and a sharp piece of Britta characterization. Britta's panic-defense ('what am I, a homophobe?') is a perfect Britta move: she reaches for her progressive identity as a shield but it proves she's deeply invested in the category. 'You so care' is a devastating two-word punctuation. This is the best Britta joke in the episode and a nice thematic resolution.

jokes.text: You are clearly just hanging out with me because you thought I was gay. So? What were you doing with me? Hey, what does it matter, you know? We're both just humans trying to make our way through this crazy world. You're the worst! And for the record, I never thought you were cool. I only thought you were a lesbian.
jokes.setup: Both women accuse each other of only hanging out for the wrong reasons
jokes.punchline: Page's 'I never thought you were cool. I only thought you were a lesbian' is the perfect mirror-image insult — Britta was using Page to feel cool, Page was using Britta for lesbian cred
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The parallel structure — Britta was using Page to feel cool, Page was using Britta to feel edgy (thinking she was a lesbian) — is thematically neat. 'I never thought you were cool. I only thought you were a lesbian.' is a perfectly balanced insult: it dismisses Britta as a person while explaining the entire relationship. The 'we're both just humans' deflection by Britta before this landing is also a good Britta moment. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Page is straight. Really? Well... When she was gay I thought it was really cool of you to make out with her. Thanks, Annie.
jokes.setup: Annie reveals to Shirley that Page is straight; Shirley comments on what she observed
jokes.punchline: Shirley's 'When she was gay I thought it was really cool of you to make out with her' implies she was fine with it because she thought it was progressive, then Britta's 'Thanks, Annie' — thanking Annie for telling Shirley — is an oddly gracious close
jokes.explanation: Shirley's conditional approval — she thought the makeout was cool specifically because she thought it was a lesbian makeout — is a funny piece of Shirley hypocrisy: she's simultaneously progressive and rules-based about it. Britta's 'Thanks, Annie' is a good button.

jokes.text: Kiss! Annie!
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the revelation, someone (possibly other students) shouts 'Kiss!' at Annie and Britta
jokes.punchline: Annie's name being called out specifically — as the target of the kiss demand — is an unexpected and uncomfortable escalation; the reaction beat to this demand completes the joke
jokes.explanation: Brief cringe beat. The 'Kiss!' chant at the dance is a familiar teen movie moment; the specificity of calling Annie's name is slightly funny. Mid-to-low tier — functional but not inventive.

jokes.text: Are you wearing my underwear? Oh. I just needed a pair while I did some laundry here. I don't have a washing machine.
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a disturbing discovery about Chang's use of his personal items
jokes.punchline: Chang is wearing Jeff's underwear — the toothbrush violation escalated to the most intimate possible garment — and his explanation (he did laundry at Jeff's apartment) adds a second layer of uninvited domesticity
jokes.explanation: The Chang boundary-violation escalation peaks here: toothbrush → underwear → laundry at Jeff's apartment. The escalating intimacy of violations is well-structured, and 'I don't have a washing machine' as an explanation-that-makes-it-worse is a good beat. Chang's blithe unawareness continues to be his best comedic mode.

jokes.text: I'm homeless, Jeff, okay? When my wife found out about Shirley and me, she kicked me out... For good this time! My whole life is in this dishwasher, man! Well, some of it's also soaking in your bathtub.
jokes.setup: Chang explains why he has no washing machine — he's been living at Jeff's apartment covertly
jokes.punchline: The cascade of revelations: (1) he's homeless, (2) wife kicked him out over Shirley, (3) his life is in the dishwasher, (4) also in Jeff's bathtub. Each adds another layer of squatting
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sustained jokes. The escalation is perfectly structured: each sentence adds a new horror. 'My whole life is in this dishwasher, man!' is a great line — the bathos of a human life stored in an appliance. The immediate qualifier 'Well, some of it's also soaking in your bathtub' is a perfect dark escalation that makes the dishwasher seem restrained. Character-specific (only Chang) and very quotable.

jokes.text: You orchestrated this entire party just so you could weasel your way into staying here! You weren't even going to notice.
jokes.setup: Jeff realizes the party was Chang's long con to establish residency
jokes.punchline: Chang's 'You weren't even going to notice' — his defense of the scheme being that it would have worked — is a perfect expression of his shamelessness
jokes.explanation: Chang's logic — 'you weren't even going to notice' as a defense of covert squatting — is a great character beat. He's not apologetic about the scheme; he's annoyed Jeff found out. The gap between the magnitude of the violation and Chang's casual response is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Hey, Jeff, don't kill the messenger, but you have four hermit crabs in your bathroom sink. You'll fall in love with them. I named one Jeff.
jokes.setup: Chang's domestic squatting is revealed to extend to live animals
jokes.punchline: Four hermit crabs in Jeff's sink — another layer of uninvited domesticity — and Chang naming one Jeff as a presumptuous act of affection
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation cap on the Chang squatting story. 'You'll fall in love with them' — Chang's confident prediction — and 'I named one Jeff' — the territorial act of affection — are both great. Naming the crab Jeff implies a level of domestic familiarity Chang feels that Jeff absolutely doesn't. High quotability and a great image. Chang's shameless optimism is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Just a month. Three... Tops. I mean... how long is your lease?
jokes.setup: Jeff demands to know how long Chang planned to stay
jokes.punchline: Chang's escalation from 'a month' to 'three tops' to 'how long is your lease?' — turning a temporary overstay into a potential permanent residency inquiry
jokes.explanation: Classic escalation joke with perfect rhythm. The three-step escalation — month / three tops / how long is your lease — takes about five seconds and conveys that Chang has been thinking much more expansively about this arrangement than 'a month.' The lease question at the end implies permanent residency ambitions. Very quotable and characteristically Chang.

jokes.text: Way to go, idiots!
jokes.setup: Jeff kicks everyone out of the party; Leonard observes the ejection
jokes.punchline: Leonard's parting shot — a heckle directed at Jeff and Duncan for not managing the party — is characteristically inappropriate and self-satisfied
jokes.explanation: Leonard gets a quick exit gag. 'Way to go, idiots!' is a good Leonard line — he's being ejected but is somehow also the authority figure passing judgment. Mid-tier but perfectly economical.

jokes.text: Star-burns, Leonard, Magnitude. Pop, pop — swizzle, scandalous, C Dubb, Tim. Mighty D. Glisten. Good night, everyone. Faster. Move it.
jokes.setup: Jeff ejects the party guests by name
jokes.punchline: The list of names — including 'swizzle, scandalous, C Dubb, Tim, Mighty D, Glisten' — reveals a roster of Greendale minor characters with absurdly colorful aliases
jokes.explanation: Jeff rattling off the names — real and street — of a ridiculous cast of Greendale peripheral characters is a great world-building joke. 'Mighty D. Glisten' and 'C Dubb' are hilariously specific inventions. The list implies Jeff knows all these people better than he admits, which is a character note. Good Community joke about the absurdity of community college social ecosystems.

jokes.text: Well, I actually started to have fun until that maniac tried to move in. What is it about me that makes broken people flock to me? Is it my height? Do huddled masses mistake me for the Statue of Liberty?
jokes.setup: Jeff reflects on the evening's events to Duncan
jokes.punchline: 'Do huddled masses mistake me for the Statue of Liberty?' — Jeff's self-aggrandizing but also self-deprecating explanation for why broken people attach to him
jokes.explanation: Jeff's 'Statue of Liberty' metaphor is both self-aggrandizing (comparing himself to a national symbol) and accurate as a description of his role in the group. The escalation from 'is it my height' to the Statue of Liberty explanation is well-structured absurdist logic. Very Jeff.

jokes.text: Is it my height? Do huddled masses mistake me for the Statue of Liberty?
jokes.setup: Jeff continues wondering why broken people are drawn to him
jokes.punchline: He speculates it might be his height — that he resembles the Statue of Liberty and 'huddled masses' come to him. The grandiosity of the self-image (comparing himself to the Statue of Liberty) is very Jeff.
jokes.explanation: Very good Jeff joke. The 'huddled masses' construction is a perfect Winger-ism — he frames his attractiveness to damaged people in grandiose historical/national monument terms. The absurdist image of people mistaking Jeff for the Statue of Liberty because of height is funny and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Well, you assume I enjoy it because you think you'd enjoy it. That's true. I am very lonely.
jokes.setup: Duncan suggests Jeff is 'starting to enjoy' his chaotic community college life; Jeff deflects with a psychological counter-argument
jokes.punchline: Duncan's response — 'That's true. I am very lonely.' — is a completely honest, vulnerable admission that lands as comedy because it's so direct and because Duncan delivers it without self-pity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The joke is in the total honesty and total lack of self-pity. Jeff makes a clever psychological point about projection; Duncan simply confirms it ('That's true') and adds the actual reason ('I am very lonely') without defense or shame. The economy is extraordinary — four words do enormous emotional and comedic work. It's also a thematic resonance with Jeff's own emotional unavailability. Duncan delivers his isolation as a fact, which is funnier and sadder than any comic performance of it would be.

jokes.text: You want a, uh, nice little taste of what you're missing in a relationship with six nutcases? Yeah! Let's turn on my phone and listen to the 39 messages they left tonight. You have no new messages.
jokes.setup: Jeff confidently proposes listening to the many messages the study group left on his phone as evidence of their codependence
jokes.punchline: 'You have no new messages.' — the group has not called at all, completely deflating Jeff's premise
jokes.explanation: The best structural joke in the episode, and among the best in the season. Jeff sets up an elaborate demonstration ('39 messages') that he intends as an argument against the group — only to have the punchline delivered by his own phone. The joke works on three levels simultaneously: (1) it's funny because his confidence is immediately demolished; (2) it reveals something true about Jeff — he WANTS to be needed, the messages were his validation; (3) it's a purely structural joke where the setup is completely recontextualized by the punchline. The '39 messages' specificity makes the silence louder. This is craft-forward Community comedy at its best.

jokes.text: Huh. That's... [beat] Huh.
jokes.setup: Jeff's phone reveals no messages; Jeff processes this
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'Huh' — Jeff's deflated non-reaction — is the comedic landing for the voicemail joke, as all his confident swagger evaporates into two syllables
jokes.explanation: The 'Huh. That's... Huh.' is a great comic beat. Jeff's verbal processing — the incomplete sentence, the pause, the second Huh — is a masterclass in comic deflation. Pure character work: Jeff Winger, master of words, reduced to a monosyllable by his own phone. The beat works because we know what he's feeling (hurt, surprised, exposed) and we watch him fail to find words for it. Perfect economy. This is inseparable from joke 79 as a two-part joke.

jokes.text: Since you've got it turned on, why don't you call me a cab and then pay for it?
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the voicemail moment, Duncan offers a practical request
